column3: It directly states that invoked beings neither hear nor answer, and disown the association.
Its movement through weakness and strength provides a secondary contrast to the focus's shared weakness.
The gathering for the Day does not clarify the test of false invocation.
The parable of competing partners versus one master sharply illuminates divided false allegiance.
The preceding local ayah names worship without warrant or knowledge, setting up the focus's demonstration.
Its request for multiplied punishment uses weakness only in a separate scene.
It contrasts taking rivals besides God with recognizing that all power belongs to God.
The following local ayah draws the conclusion that God has not been appraised according to His due.
Life, death, and final gathering add no material to the parable of incapacity.
Its command to listen gives a direct reception posture for the announced parable.
The question about rescuing one in the Fire parallels the focus's denied ability to recover what is taken.
Its preference for forgiveness over accumulation is not connected to invocation or creation.
The contrast between one unable to do anything and one enabled to give reinforces unequal capacity.
The preceding hostility to clear signs supplies a local instance of refusing the message introduced in the focus.
It explicitly denies that those invoked besides God can create anything.
It challenges the invoked to answer, directly exposing the failure of the claimed relationship.
The iron implements of punishment add no understanding of the focus's argument.
Human weakness and numerical odds are a distinct military use of the term.
It contrasts God's true judgment with the inability of those invoked besides Him to decide anything.
Divine strength and victory are broadly relevant but do not develop the parable.
The doubled reward for faith and works is unrelated to the focus's test of idols.
It directly asks false partners to show what they created, matching the focus's creation challenge.
The repeated return to punishment is not tied to false invocation or incapacity.
Creation of heaven and earth and the possibility of replacement establish the Creator's unrestricted power.
The warning of doubled punishment has no material link beyond a shared word.
Divine rescue and might offer only a broad contrast to the weakness named in the focus.
It asserts God's sole dominion, creative power, and control over all people.
Its statement that God gives parables supports the form, but not this parable's argument.
The ruined settlement image does not develop the focus's challenge to invoked beings.
The denied rescue of the drowning offers a limited parallel to inability to save.
The command to convey revelation and the denial of guidance to disbelievers are only contextual.
God's ownership of heaven and earth provides a broad sovereignty frame for rejecting rival claims.
The reversal of an oppressed group's status uses weakness in a different social setting.
Creation and command, including the ordered celestial bodies, reinforce God's governing authority.
The destruction of prior deniers gives only a general consequence for rejection.
God's creation of an individual offers a minimal creator theme without the invocation argument.
It repeats the demand that those invoked besides God show what they created.
Its generic contrast of falsehood and truth through parables is secondary to the focus.
The garden parable and weak descendants concern a different moral warning.
The legal compensation for game uses likeness without advancing the focus's claim.
The people's calling Shu'ayb weak gives a social contrast, not divine incapacity.
Creation of dispersed living creatures supports the focus's appeal to a small living creature as a sign.
It denies that alternative gods can avert harm or rescue, closely matching the focus's failed recourse.
The warning not to repeat a slander does not illuminate the parable.
Creation named at the opening of revelation is only a broad premise.
The passage's false listening and rejected judgment offer only a distant reception parallel.
It presents listening and following the best of speech, a substantive counterpart to hearing the parable.
Its dispute between the arrogant and the oppressed uses weakness in another setting.
It shows that association with righteous servants cannot protect those who betray, limiting claimed support.
The question whether clan honor outweighs God illustrates misplaced regard but only indirectly.
The exposure of weaker supporters and fewer numbers is a secondary comparison of strength.
It says wrongdoers cannot avail one another against God, contrasting failed mutual protection with divine guardianship.
Creation is invoked only as the source of feared evil, without the focus's argument.
The claim that disbelief cannot harm God gives a broad divine-independence contrast.
The subjection of all in heaven and earth supports God's comprehensive authority over creation.
It joins the use of parables with many people's refusal, clarifying a possible response to the focus's example.
The assertion that God created people presses the recognition of the true Creator.
It directly tests those invoked besides God for their inability to remove harm or withhold mercy.
Creation of male and female supplies only a general creator theme.
The debt-writing rules do not contribute to the focus's parable.
The gathered Day is not materially connected to the focus's creation and recovery test.
Its direct question whether the objects of invocation hear them is a close counterpart.
Future exposure of the weaker party and force gives a limited strength contrast.
Its tree parable establishes parabolic form but addresses a different subject.
God's creating and choosing are set against association, reinforcing exclusive divine agency.
The people's reaction to a parable gives only a general reception parallel.
The filling of Hell with followers gives a broad consequence for following falsehood.
The exchange of blame between arrogant and weak groups is a distant parallel to failed dependence.
God's creation of all on earth and the heavens is a broad creator frame already well represented.
It denies that wealth or children can avail disbelievers against God, another limit on supposed resources.
Taking Satan as a patron and altering creation is only indirectly related to false allegiance.
Universal divine dominion and the call to believe offer a general monotheistic frame.
It highlights the inconsistency of admitting God as Creator while being turned away.
The demand for a sign and its threatened abasement are only a secondary rejection parallel.
The collective descent and guidance promise do not develop the focus's argument.
Collective attachment to God's rope and rescue from fire offer only a distant dependence contrast.
Human common origin supports creation generally but adds little after stronger creator passages.
The groups gathered in Hell and their mutual accusations are a remote parallel to shared weakness.
Exemption for the weak and ill concerns legal obligation, not the focus's incapacity.
The inability to retrieve lost water offers a concise parallel to the focus's inability to recover what is taken.
Its question whether people create or God creates directly supports the focus's creation test.
Universal belief under divine will is a broad sovereignty point, not an idol-incapacity argument.
Individual responsibility and final return do not clarify the parable.
Its parable of a tiny creature and the divided response to it closely illuminates the focus's small-creature example.
God's creation of people and what they do is a broad agency claim already covered by more direct cards.
The prohibition on alliance with a despairing people does not add to the focus.
The weak followers' failed appeal to the arrogant exposes the collapse of dependent protection.
It explicitly says those invoked besides God do not answer and illustrates futile calling.
It notes that people acknowledge the Creator of heaven and earth, sharpening the inconsistency behind other invocation.
The garden parable about spending has no relevant capacity or invocation theme.
The isolated address does not add a usable connection.
The wish to ransom oneself with everyone on earth does not develop the focus.
Its hearing without understanding and rejection of every sign supplies a reception contrast to the command to listen.
The designation of the Lord as continual Creator and knowing reinforces the divine side of the creation contrast.
The detailed law of accidental killing is unrelated to the focus.
The call to observe how a creature was created supports reflection on created life only broadly.
Its testimony to the sole deity gives the doctrinal conclusion opposed to calling rivals besides God.
The stages of human formation offer a secondary instance of divine creating and shaping.
Regret for disobeying God and the messenger offers a general consequence for misdirected obedience.
The piling and gathering of evil for Hell gives only a distant collective-outcome contrast.
It asks whether rivals are associated despite creating nothing and themselves being created.
It denies that the invoked can help their callers or help themselves.
It challenges alleged partners to show comparable creation, directly testing rival creative agency.
Its question whether the Creator is like one who does not create supplies the focus's governing contrast.
It denies that beings worshipped besides God possess provision or any capacity.
It tells people to call alleged rivals, then denies their power to remove or alter harm.
It identifies taking gods besides God in expectation of strength, directly framing the focus's false dependence.
It says those supposed gods will deny their worship and turn against their devotees.
It asks whether the calf could answer, control harm, or provide benefit.
Abraham asks why people worship what neither benefits nor harms them.
It rejects worship besides God when the objects have no understanding or effective power.
It describes calling what neither harms nor benefits, a direct counterpart to the focus's invocation critique.
It continues by naming the invoked object as nearer to harm than benefit and a wretched patron.
It forbids calling another god without proof, giving the doctrinal boundary for the focus's example.
It describes gods besides Him that create nothing, are created, and control neither harm nor benefit.
It completes the question about idols by asking whether they benefit or harm.
Its challenge about originating and restoring creation culminates in the question of any god alongside God.
It says that those worshipped besides God do not control provision, exposing their dependence.
It denies that alleged partners possess even the smallest share of the heavens or earth.
The angels disavow being worshipped, showing the invoked party's repudiation of false devotion.
It asks whether any creator other than God provides from heaven and earth.
It notes that people take gods besides God in hopes of receiving help.
It immediately denies that those gods can help, reversing the expected support relation.
It assigns all intercession exclusively to God, restricting a central claimed function of rivals.
It limits intercession for those called besides Him, subjecting it to truth and knowledge.
It calls the most astray those who invoke beings besides God that will not answer until the Day.
Its naming of the prominent goddesses opens a direct critique of claimed divine rivals.
It characterizes those named rivals as names without authority, clarifying the lack of warrant behind invocation.
